title: Persian cat
wiki_lead:
The Persian cat, also known as the Persian Longhair or simply Persian, is a long-haired traditional breed of cat characterised by a round face and petite, but not flat and not smashed in, muzzle. The short flat nose was created in the US from in-breeding and causes breathing difficulties in the breed, whereas the traditional Persian breed has a petite nose which enables them to breathe without difficulties. 
The first Persian cats may have been brought to Italy from Khorasan as early as 1620, but  there is stronger evidence for a longhaired cat breed exported from Afghanistan and Iran/Persia from the 19th century onwards. Persian cats have been widely recognised by the North-West European cat fancy since the 19th century, and after World War II by breeders from North America, Australia and New Zealand. Some cat fancier organisations' breed standards subsume the Himalayan and Exotic Shorthair as variants of this breed, while others generally treat them as separate breeds.
The selective breeding carried out by breeders has allowed the development of a wide variety of coat colours, but has also led to the creation of increasingly flat-faced Persian cats. Favoured by fanciers, this head structure can bring with it several health problems. As is the case with the Siamese breed, there have been efforts by some breeders to preserve the older type of cat, the Traditional Persian, which has a more pronounced muzzle. Hereditary polycystic kidney disease (PKD) is prevalent in the breed, affecting almost half of the population in some countries.
In 2021, Persian cats were ranked as the fourth-most popular cat breed in the world according to the Cat Fanciers' Association (CFA), a US-based international cat registry.

History


Origin
The exact time of the appearance of long-haired cats is unclear, as no long-haired specimens of the African wildcat, the ancestor of the domestic cat species, are known.

The first documented ancestors of the Persian cat might have been imported from Khorasan, either Eastern Iran or Western Afghanistan, into the Italian Peninsula in 1620 by Pietro Della Valle; and from Damascus, Syria, into France by Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc at around the same time. While the de Peiresc import from Syria is corroborated by later correspondences, Della Valle is only known to have voiced his intention in a letter from 1620 but returned to Italy much later in 1626 after travelling several other countries with the remains of his wife in tow and no further mention of the cats.
In his letter from 1620, Della Valle distinguishes the Khorasan cat from similar long-haired cats imported to Europe from the Near East by their grey coat:

At this point I have found in this country a very beautiful species of cats which are native to the province of Khorasan, but of another appearance and quality than those of Tyre, Lebanon. grok_lead: The Persian (also known as the Persian Longhair) is a long-haired breed of domestic cat characterized by a round face and massive, rounded head with a short, flat muzzle, small ears, large round eyes, a stocky body with short legs often appearing compact or huddled due to its build, and a dense, long, fluffy coat in various colors including cream (light orange) that requires extensive grooming. Known for its calm, affectionate, and docile temperament, the breed thrives in quiet household environments where it can receive ample attention. Originating from long-haired cats imported from Persia and surrounding regions to Europe in the 17th century, the modern Persian was developed through selective breeding in the 19th century to emphasize its signature luxurious fur and facial structure. This conformation has contributed to its enduring popularity as one of the top pedigree cat breeds worldwide, ranking third in ownership statistics as of 2024. However, the extreme brachycephalic featuresâresulting from intensive artificial selectionâpredispose Persians to significant health challenges, including respiratory obstruction, ocular disorders, dental malocclusion, polycystic kidney disease, and dermatological issues, with studies documenting elevated disorder prevalence compared to other breeds. These hereditary conditions underscore causal links between exaggerated morphology and impaired welfare, prompting calls for breeding reforms to prioritize health over aesthetics in reputable registries.
